Author: @paintedcrow
Content:
Just did some back-of-the-napkin statistics. My numbers suggest that a team of four reviewers is likely to collectively miss one out of every few hundred "obvious" errors, even if they're all doing their best.

Assumptions behind these calculations include: even the very best copyeditors only catch about 90% of errors, and good copyeditors DO check for things like arithmetic errors, so that's a decent place to start. Academics are generally overworked and underpaid, not all of them are super skilled editors, they're probably focused on finding more subtle errors like issues with flaky methodology, and people are human and sometimes they're sick or jetlagged, so I'm going to estimate that they're probably clustering around 75% to 80% accuracy. Totally made up number, but it sounds arbitrarily reasonable.

Glaring ignorance behind these calculations includes: I have no idea how many reviewers typically look over academic papers or if that varies by journal, and I also don't know if they play different roles in terms of what they're looking for. This could easily set this calculation off by (ha!) an order of magnitude.

So, roughly estimating that each error has a certain chance of being caught by each of four reviewers... If the reviewers are all pretty solid, each catching 80% of errors, it's a 1 in 625 chance that any given "obvious" error will be missed by all of them.

If you have a team who's worn out by deadlines, lack of sleep, the flu (easy to get sick after conferences), or jetlag, or some are just younger and less experienced at their job—say one has an 80% chance of catching errors, one 75%, one 70%, and one's not doing so hot and is down to 60%... you're up to a 1 in 167 chance that any given error will be missed by this team.

These are still low odds on the whole! Academics typically take a lot of pride in their work and care about getting it right (otherwise they'd be in a much less stressful, better-paying job), so the number of meaningful errors like this left in a paper BEFORE it gets to the reviewers won't be super high. But with how many studies are published each year, something will slip through eventually even if everyone involved is genuinely doing their best.

Scientists are human too. Give 'em some patience.

Author: @needsmoreboosters4264
Content: Early-career chemist here. One of the reasons I chose to go into industry rather than pursuing further academics and research (at least at the moment) is what science has become in the last decade or two... the excessive monetization of journals and other essential materials, the restriction of paper access to the general public, and the fact that scientists are judged almost purely on what they publish, hurts the scientific community by incentivizing institutions to push out low-quality research with less-than-adequate review. It sets us back and absolutely hurts the public trust in science as a whole whenever a research scandal like this comes to light. We need to focus more on the quality of our data, and on educating the general public about the scientific method and about how the data they eventually see is actually obtained, so that they understand why these mistakes are made and can be part of the solution rather than turning to pseudoscience or conspiracies. That being said, I do still believe science is the best way we have of obtaining factual information. We just still have a lot of work to do, especially in removing the monetary influence and corruption from the system.

Author: @AllelineMuse
Content: I think you're confused between "people who are skeptical of scientific results" and "people who don't like to be bullied by scientific results".  Any scientifically literate person would read scientific results with a healthy dose of skepticism, which is what allows people to spot simple arithmetic errors in the first place.  Reading scientific results critically and being skeptical is a normal part of scientific discourse.  However, it is becoming increasingly fashionable to use the name of "science" to bully people, where people will claim that something is "true" (in the absolutist sense) just because it's published in a scientific paper, and if you don't believe them then you must be on the side of the "enemy".  I think it's perfectly fine and reasonable that people don't automatically trust the first thing they read in a scientific paper; and in fact, it's also fine to not trust or agree with the "scientific consensus", as long as they actually understand what they're disagreeing with.  There's nothing magical about the scientific process that makes its conclusion automatically "true".  Science is still the BEST method we have to reaching toward objective "truth", but it is by no means perfect, and people are perfectly legitimate to disagree with it or bet against it at their own risk.  Ascribing to a certain scientific view does not make someone more "moral" or right, but it's simply a difference in how we interpret the data and risks.

Author: @SolaAesir
Content:
You are right that this sort of error is a fairly inconsequential issue, something that happens from time to time. You also shouldn't be trusting people without the requisite scientific training. You should probably put more trust in the people who do have the requisite training though, even if your interaction with them is in a science communication context rather than through reading a journal article. The rest of your rant is complete BS though. 

Any time you hear that peer review is a fundamental part of how science is done, you should translate that in your head into "Brawndo is what plants crave. It's got electrolytes." If you aren't familiar with the history of science publication, the editors of scientific journals used to be highly paid, well respected scientists getting near the end of their careers. That turned out to be too expensive, so the journals made a big advertising campaign to switch out the highly paid, competent people whose names and reputations were on the line for unpaid labor who will try to take a glance at those 5 papers you sent them when they have a couple of spare minutes. Stuff like this is exactly the sort of thing that peer review is supposed to catch most easily and, as you can see, it just doesn't. This isn't even the worst example. Go through papers in quite a few fields and you'll find published studies that wouldn't pass a high school science fair. Several fields are having giant replication crises with foundational work turning out to have been fabricated. 

The thing is, we already have a better model and it's what scientists themselves use: arXiv. Scientists have to read papers in their field of study daily anyway, just put comments attached to the papers and you already have a much more powerful system than peer review. We've seen it in action quite a few times with fast moving discoveries/situations. The problem is, no journals make big money for providing zero value under that system, so there's a lot of advertising against it (along with blacklists against scientists who suggest such notions). Just look up Aaron Schwartz if you think that's an idle threat.

Hey Adam. I’ve been following you since the lockdowns.
Initially for the cooking, and now more and more also for your scientific editorializing (that’s the best term I’ve been able to come up with 😅).

This essay is really, really spot on. There’s such a, well, strange set of convictions about “science” among so many people. There’s this belief (and I think that’s the appropriate term) that science is like faith. That it’s something you have to take on faith, as a block, as a whole.
You either believe in Jesus, Allah, Yahweh, Şiva, … or you don’t. But if you do, you have to believe in the whole spiel, take it or leave it. And supposedly, science is similar. You’re supposed to (according to these people) believe in “science” as an all-knowing, all-seeing ‘thing’. And if, heaven forbid (yeah, I know 😏) there’s a mistake, or the scientific process of continuous improvement does what it’s supposed to do and begets new insights, those same ‘believer’ people will be shouting at the top of their digital voices that “science” is WRONG WRONG WONG!!!

Yes, it’s about trust as a first priority. Absolutely 💯 
Only it’s not limited to trust in individuals. It’s also, and maybe mostly, trust in the process itself.
That’s what differentiates science from faith.

Thank you Adam 🙏🙏🙏

Author: @CanIBorrowYourShovel
Content:
The way I explain this to people is this: "do not let healthy skepticism become blind conspiratorial mistrust".

I have a huge problem with pay walling knowledge of research. I also think there is not enough transparency in peer review, with some authors getting very lenient review and opening up a pressure to abuse the system, like with the recent bombshell megastar psychology researchers at Stanford and others being only recently caught fabricating evidence for decades. I have a problem with the lack of funding for replication studies because they don't generate big showy results. And I have a huge problem with how bad scholarly writing is. It's just abominably obtuse and excessively dense and filled with meaningless jargon that is not necessary to understand or even follow the flow of the writing (especially in my field of biochemistry) with a deliberate "style" that many authors feel they need to have in order to be taken seriously. I sometimes will completely plain language rewrite a paper if I want to explain it to someone. When I wrote scholarly research, I deliberately used plain language and limited use of acronyms and prior knowledge. And I tested it by having friends and family read them and see if they can understand and repeat it back to me. Because that should be the point of academic writing. Spreading knowledge.

Because when you don't speak clearly in research, you open the door for bad actors to deliberately misconstrue your findings or intents (hence a big problem with pop science taking things out of context that the cited research wasn't even studying and find correlation or causation where none was implied)

But overall, yeah, we could be doing a lot worse. But we need to do better in a lot of ways too.

Everything needs to be investigated as thoroughly as possible, by as many people as possible, as many times as possible.

Newton's law of gravity stood for 200 years. It was known to be flawed for 100 of those 200 years. But nobody had anything that was less wrong, and nobody had anything that was more in line with observations... until Einstein had a brain spark. Einstein's general relativity is now also under scrutiny because some measurements suggest that it is incomplete. Nothing is "fact". There is only "The current theory that conflicts the least with observations".

Author: @drewjordan14
Content:
I agree with the main thrust of this video, but I think it's also helpful to acknowledge that there are legitimate criticisms of the peer review process from both inside and outside of academia. In my view, the most glaring flaw is the insistence on crafting a consistent narrative to a research paper that incentivizes not publishing contradictory data that is produced by the publishing author/lab. From the earliest point in which I got involved in academic research as an undergraduate, I noticed an emphasis on the idea of 'telling a story' within a research paper. If a researcher chooses to include results that would contradict/complicate the hypothesis in their initial submission, they will likely get slammed by reviewers and are much less likely to have their paper published in that journal.  There is generally much, much more data that is generated during the research process than what ends up being published in the limited set of figures that are allotted to researchers in the final paper.

This is obviously a difficult concept to convey to a lay audience without the potential for creating a disproportionate backlash of distrust in the scientific process, but I think it's still a worthwhile conversation to have.

My point also does not mention the fact that peer review is a time consuming and somewhat unrewarded duty for scientists that places an onerous task on researchers that already have more responsibilities than what I think should be considered reasonable of scientists—all the while scientific journals rake in millions from costly publishing fees (which are even higher if a researcher wants to publish open access) and university subscriptions.

Author: @robonator2945
Content:
I'd honestly disagree, if you're going to make a claim about this sort of stuff and you're that close to the tipping point you should absolutely be doing that math 5 times over and asking a friend to do the same math again without showing them yours. Basically any result that's within an order of magnitude should be taken with 5 tons of salt until verified, reverified, and verified again. IMO a big issue with the modern scientific culture is "well it passes the bar for statistical significance if we test it like this". The truth is you can eek out marginal correlations in basically any data you find, so unless you have a 2% correlation with a 99% confidence that's consistent across all 20 of your different methods of measurement, it's as good as meaningless as far as I'm concerned. Things like CI can only filter out *_random_* variances, but if your approach has fundamental biases they can't do shit. Now, if you have a 70% correlation? Yeah, alright, then maybe you don't need *_as many_* checks, but if you're barely cracking the reference dose then you had better be double checking yourself to make absolutely sure you're right. 

This isn't just when it comes to 'proper science' either, but tons of different fields. For instance Kyle Hill somewhat recently made a video on the atomic manhole cover where he got a result that was within an order of magnitude using some incredibly rough approximations and then decided that the entire thing must not be true. When you're using math *_that_* rough, one order of magnitude is the bar to beat, and his numbers didn't pass it. When making any decision, anywhere in your life, you stack all the cards against yourself, then see if you get the result you want. If you did? Great! Now you can be damn near certain your decision is correct. If not? Okay, now repeat it again peeling back layer upon layer of aggressive assumptions. How many benefits of the doubt can you NOT give yourself before you get the result you want? 100? 50? 25? 15? 10? 5? 1? A truly correct and meaningful result should be obvious well, WELL before the tipping point of 'fairness'. Now that's not *_always_* true, but it's a hell of a lot easier to triple vet the handful of times when it isn't then constantly be wrong all the times that it is. 

Way too many people today just completely fail to understand that you always stack the deck against yourself if you care about being right. Anyone can win when they're counting cards, but only the absolute best can win even while they're counting stars.

Content:
That's the point of the scientific method. It's a process where you, I, we, distrust everyone and everybody. Starting with the researcher distrusting themselves when they are doing research. That's exactly what some politicians, and flat earthers, and homeopathic sellers, and mediums, and faith healers, and little angry orange nazis, and witches, and all the others do NOT do: you can't replicate their findings, and they hide as much of their processes and ways as possible. And they don't correct their mistakes when found out, they just lie and move on to the next grift. 
The processes of the scientific method is what was proven to be trustworthy, to be the best we have; it weeds out errors and mistakes over time, and push the best answers available to the top.  And it's done by all of us, collectively; but especially by others scientists who review and reproduce the work of their peers.

Author: @absentmindedjwc
Content:
I’ve absolutely seen people use this as a reason to “distrust science,” when this is literally how science works. Science isn’t about unwavering trust in a claim - it’s about testing that claim over and over. If new evidence comes along that challenges it, the claim is re-evaluated, and if the research proves it wrong, it’s replaced with a better, more accurate understanding.

It drives me nuts that so many people seem to have slept through their science classes. This is literally the scientific method in action. The fact that our understanding evolves isn’t a weakness; it’s the whole point. Science isn’t about blind belief - that’s dogma. Science is about questioning, testing, and constantly improving what we know. If people understood that, maybe they’d stop acting like a shifting understanding is some kind of betrayal instead of what it’s supposed to be.

Author: @TheGlitchyCorgi
Content:
The real moral: don't trust "fad" science stories that gets blared out of every media outlet.
Real science is hard. It takes time. I takes more than one study to prove that a thing is so.
After 5-10 years and another half-dozen studies have looked at the same issue, if they all come to the same general conclusion in properly peer-reviewed papers, then yes, you can reasonably trust that result. Till then, don't put too much stock in the latest sensational study getting trotted around.
